title: Faith and reason
hook: Christians have long held both are gifts from the same God

segments.voice: Yesterday, angry at God: the psalms, Job and Jeremiah argue with him out loud. Your line was he can take it. Did you say one honest, angry thing, to God or to the dark? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-two.

A Bible study, a Tuesday night, folding chairs in a circle. A teenager in the back raises her hand and asks the question others in the room have been sitting on: if I keep asking questions, does that mean I don't have enough faith? Nobody answers right away. It's an old worry, that thinking hard is the opposite of believing, that the mind is a door you close before you kneel. A line of Christian thinkers answers that worry with a no. Faith and reason, they say, come from the same God, and he isn't afraid of either one. Today: faith and reason.

Start with Jesus. Asked for the great commandment, he answers in the King James words: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind." The mind is on the list. Thinking is one of the ways love is given. Then the prophet Isaiah, where God himself opens what sounds like a case at law: "Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD." An invitation to talk it through. Then a small scene in the book of Acts. Paul arrives in a town called Berea and preaches. The people there, Acts says, "received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so." They checked the apostle's preaching against the scrolls. And the text doesn't scold them for it. It calls them more noble. Then a letter of Peter asks Christians to "be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear." A reason, and a gentle one. Later Christians kept building on this. Anselm of Canterbury described his work as faith seeking understanding: faith goes first, then goes looking. Pope John Paul II began a letter on this subject with a picture: faith and reason are like two wings, and the human spirit rises on both toward the truth. Christians weigh the two wings differently. Some put real trust in how far reason can reach toward God on its own. Others stress how easily a human mind wanders, and lean harder on what God reveals. But in the texts here, nobody is asked to switch the mind off. A bird with one wing doesn't get far.

Here's the practice: think carefully about one belief. Settle, and breathe. Pick one thing you hold to be true, about God or about anything: that people are mostly good, that prayer matters, that there's nothing after death. Ask it three plain questions. Where did I first get this? Why do I still hold it? What would I say if a friend asked me for the reason? You don't have to change it, and you don't have to win an argument. Just look at it in good light, the way the Bereans unrolled the scrolls. If you pray, you can ask for an honest mind. The bell holds the time.
Faith and reason. Trust and careful thinking, which the Christian thinkers in today's lesson call gifts of the same God, meant to fly together.

Your line: two wings. Today, when a hard question comes up, about faith or about anything else, don't shut the door on it. Ask it out loud, and go looking for an honest answer. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Christians bring faith and reason together in Bible study groups, catechism classes, theology and apologetics; Catholic teaching in particular has written at length on how the two work together, and Protestant and Orthodox churches each have their own traditions of careful thinking about faith.

original.note: Greek: mind, understanding — the word behind "with all thy mind" in Matthew 22:37.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith means not asking questions.
what it means: the Bible names the mind as a way to love God, and praises the people who checked what they were told.
what a scholar hears: Anselm's fides quaerens intellectum, faith seeking understanding. faith goes first, and then it goes looking.

sources.work: Pope John Paul II, Fides et Ratio

notes: Fides et Ratio's opening image (faith and reason as two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth) is paraphrased, not quoted; the encyclical's English text is not public domain. Confirm paraphrase.
'Faith seeking understanding' (fides quaerens intellectum) attributed to Anselm, from the Proslogion; confirm.
Isaiah 1:18 in context is a courtroom-style dispute; 'like someone pulling up a chair' is a light image. Confirm it doesn't soften the passage too much.

The two emphases (trust in natural reason vs. stress on reason's limits and on revelation) are described without naming churches; Keeper may want to name them (e.g. Catholic natural theology, some Reformed emphases) or leave as is.
